source_text: Φεύγετε οὖν τὰς κακὰς παραφυάδας τὰς γεννώσας καρπὸν θανατηφόρον, οὗ ἐὰν γεύσηταί τις, παῤ αὐτὰ ἀποθνήσκει. οὗτοι γὰρ οὔκ εἰσιν φυτεία πατρός, 2, εἰ γὰρ ἦσαν, ἐφαίνοντο ἂν κλάδοι τοῦ σταυροῦ, καὶ ἦν ἂν ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῶν ἄφθαρτος: δἰ οὗ ἐν τῷ πάθει αὐτοῦ προσκαλεῖταν ὑμᾶς ὄντας μέλη αὐτοῦ. οὐ δύναται οὖν κεφαλὴ χωρὶς γεννηθῆναι ἄνευ μελῶν, τοῦ θεοῦ ἕνωσιν ἐπαγγελλομένου, ὅ ἐστιν αὐτός.
thought_title: Flee the deadly offshoots; be branches of the cross
orientation: Ignatius is warning the Trallians against teachers who deny the real suffering of Christ, and now tells them to flee these false teachers because they are not God's planting.
pass_a_gloss: Flee therefore the evil offshoots, the ones producing fruit death-bringing, of which if anyone tastes, immediately he dies. For these are not a planting of the Father; for if they were, they would have appeared as branches of the cross, and their fruit would have been imperishable; through which in his passion he calls you to himself, you being his members. A head therefore cannot be born separately without members, God promising unity, which is himself.

choices.why: The image is of shoots growing off a plant, false growths that are not part of the true planting; 'offshoots' keeps the botanical metaphor.
The genitive πατρός is possessive; the phrase echoes the biblical image of God's planting, and 'planting' keeps the noun form of the metaphor.
The cross is pictured as a tree from which true believers grow as branches; 'branches of the cross' preserves the striking image.
The middle voice has a personal force: Christ summons believers into union with himself; 'calls you to himself' captures the direction of the call.
The glossary fixes ἕνωσις as 'unity'; the participle is causal or explanatory, giving the reason the head cannot be born without members.

pass_b_english: So flee from these evil offshoots that produce death-bringing fruit. If anyone tastes it, he dies on the spot. These people are not a planting of the Father. If they were, they would show themselves as branches of the cross, and their fruit would be imperishable. Through the cross, in his passion, he calls you, who are his members. A head cannot come to be without members, since God promises unity, and that unity is himself.

problems.quote: Through the cross Christ in his passion calls you to himself, since you are his members.
problems.source_quote: δὲ ἐν τῷ πάθει αὐτοῦ προσκαλεῖται ὑμᾶς ὄντας μέλη αὐτοῦ.
problems.why: Greek says only that in his passion he calls you as his members; English adds “Through the cross” and “to himself” which are not in the source.
problems.fix: In his passion he calls you, being his members.
problems.ruling: Source has no 'διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ' or 'πρὸς ἑαυτόν'; translator adds 'Through the cross' and 'to himself,' changing meaning.

edits.old: Through the cross Christ in his passion calls you to himself, since you are his members.
edits.new: In his passion he calls you, being his members.

last_rejected.quote: In his passion he calls you, being his members.
last_rejected.source_quote: δἰ οὗ ἐν τῷ πάθει αὐτοῦ προσκαλεῖταν ὑμᾶς ὄντας μέλη αὐτοῦ
last_rejected.why: The relative pronoun δι᾽ οὗ ('through which') referring back to the cross is omitted; the English reads as if 'in his passion' alone is the means.
last_rejected.fix: Through which, in his passion, he calls you, being his members.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek adds ‘through which’ linking to the cross; English still conveys the call in his passion, omission doesn’t alter core meaning.

polish.changed: Clarified the head and members metaphor by rendering 'born' as 'come to be' and connecting the cross to Christ's call, making the sentence flow naturally while preserving every claim.

notes.quote: A head cannot be born without members
notes.why: Heads are not 'born' with or without members; the metaphor is mixed and unclear.
notes.fix: Render as 'A head cannot exist without its members' or 'A head is not complete without members.'
